title: Bài sưu tầm 134 - Passage 1: The Wild Leaf: How Tea Cultivation Transformed Assam
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1 — TEST 134

The Wild Leaf: How Tea Cultivation Transformed Assam

Paragraph 1. At the dawn of the nineteenth century, Britain's growing appetite for tea depended entirely on China. Chinese merchants demanded payment in vast amounts of silver, draining British reserves and prompting colonial officials to seek a reliable source inside India. Leading botanists insisted that cool Himalayan slopes offered the only realistic climate, dismissing the hot, swampy plains of Assam in northeastern India as unsuitable.

Paragraph 2. Yet in 1823, Scottish trader Robert Bruce heard rumours of a native tea tree growing wild in Assam's jungles. A local Singpho chief, Beesa Gam, showed Bruce the wild bushes and gave him dried leaves alongside a handful of seeds. Bruce died the following year, long before colonial botanists officially confirmed that his specimens belonged to the true tea species.

Paragraph 3. Even after formal verification in 1834, officials remained suspicious of the wild Indian variety. They imported eighty thousand bushes and skilled processors from China to establish model gardens. Ironically, the delicate Chinese plants withered in Assam’s scorching humidity and violent monsoon downpours, while the rugged native Assam bush thrived effortlessly.

Paragraph 4. Turning dense forest into commercial estates demanded enormous labour. Planters recruited impoverished labourers from central India and put them to work clearing mosquito-ridden wetlands, where deadly outbreaks of malaria routinely devastated newly arrived workforces.

Paragraph 5. Moving fragile tea chests out of remote valleys proved equally daunting. For decades, harvested crates were loaded onto flat-bottomed wooden barges that drifted slowly down the Brahmaputra River toward Calcutta, exposing leaves to dampness for months. Transit times only dropped sharply once paddle steamers and a narrow-gauge railway connected inland plantations directly to coastal ports.

Paragraph 6. By the 1880s, dark, malty Assam tea had overtaken Chinese imports in London's auctions. Rising production lowered retail prices, turning an aristocratic luxury into an everyday staple inside ordinary British households.

groups.title: Questions 8–13
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 1: "demanded payment in vast amounts of silver" (consumed huge amounts = demanded vast amounts).
Đoạn 2: "gave him dried leaves alongside a handful of seeds".
Đoạn 4: "outbreaks of malaria routinely devastated newly arrived workforces".

q8.text: Leading British botanists immediately recommended Assam as the most promising region for tea.

steps: Đoạn 1: Các nhà thực vật học hàng đầu cho rằng vùng đồi Himalaya mát mẻ mới khả thi và gạt bỏ Assam vì nóng ẩm.

q9.text: Robert Bruce did not live to see experts confirm his wild plants were genuine tea.

steps: Đoạn 2: "Bruce died the following year, long before colonial botanists officially confirmed that his specimens belonged to the true tea species."

q10.text: Tea bushes imported from China adapted more successfully to Assam's soil than native bushes.

steps: Đoạn 3: Cây trà Trung Quốc bị héo úa trước nắng nóng mưa mùa, trong khi giống bản địa Assam mọc khỏe tự nhiên.

q11.text: Chinese tea artisans brought to Assam received higher pay than workers recruited from central India.

steps: Đoạn 3 & 4: Bài có nhắc tuyển nghệ nhân Trung Quốc và tuyển lao động từ miền Trung Ấn Độ, nhưng hoàn toàn không so sánh tiền lương giữa hai nhóm.

q12.text: By the 1880s, Assam tea was selling in larger volumes on the British market than Chinese tea.

steps: Đoạn 6: "By the 1880s, dark, malty Assam tea had overtaken Chinese imports in London's auctions."

q13.text: British drinkers favoured Assam tea primarily because its strong taste mixed well with milk.

steps: Đoạn 6: Bài mô tả trà Assam đậm vị mạch nha và vượt trà Trung Quốc, nhưng không đề cập việc pha sữa có phải lý do chính khiến người Anh ưa chuộng hay không.
